text: BOOK I
Preface

1. Wherever Ptolemy son of Lagus and Aristobulus son of Aristobulus have written the same things about Alexander son of Philip, I record them as wholly true; where their accounts differ, I have chosen the version that seemed to me the more trustworthy and at the same time the more worth telling.

2. Others, to be sure, have written about Alexander, and there is no one about whom the writers are more numerous or more at variance with one another. But Ptolemy and Aristobulus seemed to me the more reliable in their narrative: Aristobulus because he served on Alexander's campaigns, and Ptolemy because, besides campaigning with him, he was himself a king, so that lying would have been more shameful for him than for any other man; and both because they wrote when Alexander was already dead, when neither necessity nor the hope of reward could move them to set down anything otherwise than as it happened.

3. Some things recorded by others I have set down as well, where they seemed to me worth relating and not wholly incredible, but only as things said of Alexander. And whoever wonders why, after so many writers, it occurred to me too to compose this history, let him first read through all of theirs, and then come upon mine, and only then wonder.
Chapter 1

1. It is said that Philip died in the archonship of Pythodelus at Athens, and that Alexander, the son of Philip, then about twenty years of age, succeeded to the kingdom and at once went into the Peloponnese.

2. There he gathered the Greeks within the Peloponnese and asked of them the command of the expedition against the Persians, which they had already granted to Philip. He received it from all save the Lacedaemonians, who replied that it was not their ancestral custom to follow others, but rather to lead. The city of the Athenians, too, made some show of revolt.

3. But the Athenians, dismayed at Alexander's first approach, granted him even greater honours than they had bestowed on Philip. He then returned to Macedonia and busied himself with preparations for the crossing into Asia.

4. At the beginning of spring he marched towards Thrace, against the Triballians and Illyrians, since he had learned that the Illyrians and Triballians were stirring; and as they were his neighbours, it seemed unwise to leave them behind, anything less than wholly subdued, when he was setting out so far from home.

5. Setting out from Amphipolis, he invaded that part of Thrace held by the Thracians called independent, keeping the city of Philippi and Mount Orbelus on his left. Crossing the river Nestus, on the tenth day, they say, he reached Mount Haemus.

6. There, at the narrows of the ascent to the mountain, he was met by many armed traders and by the independent Thracians, who had occupied the summit of the Haemus, by which the army's passage lay, prepared to bar his advance.

7. They had gathered wagons and set them in front of themselves, both to use as a palisade from which to fight off the Macedonians if pressed, and intending also to launch the wagons down upon the Macedonian phalanx where the slope was steepest, as the enemy climbed. Their plan was that the more densely packed the phalanx the wagons struck as they hurtled down, the more violently they would scatter it by the force of their fall.

8. Alexander took thought how he might cross the mountain most safely; and since the venture seemed unavoidable, there being no other way through, he gave orders to the hoplites that, when the wagons came rushing down the slope, those for whom the breadth of the road allowed should open their ranks and let the wagons pass through;

9. but those who were caught in a narrow place should crouch together, or even fall to the ground, and lock their shields close, so that the wagons bearing down upon them, leaping over by their momentum, as was likely, should pass without harm. And it fell out just as Alexander had advised and foreseen.

10. Some opened the phalanx, and the wagons that rolled over the shields did little harm; not a man perished beneath them. Then the Macedonians, taking heart because the wagons they had most dreaded proved harmless to them, fell upon the Thracians with a shout.

11. Alexander ordered the archers from the right wing to advance before the rest of the phalanx, since the ground was easier there, and to shoot at the Thracians wherever they pressed forward; while he himself, taking the royal guard, the hypaspists, and the Agrianians, led on by the left.

12. Then the archers, shooting down the Thracians who ran out in front, checked them; and the phalanx, closing in, easily drove from the ground men who were light-armed and ill-equipped barbarians, so that they no longer stood to receive Alexander as he led on from the left, but flung away their weapons each as he could and fled down the mountain.

13. About fifteen hundred of them were killed, though few men were taken alive, owing to their swiftness and their knowledge of the country; but all the women who accompanied them were captured, along with the children and all the plunder.
Chapter 2

1. Alexander sent the booty back to the cities on the coast, handing it over to Lysanias and Philotas to dispose of. He himself crossed the summit and advanced through the Haemus into the country of the Triballians, and came to the river Lyginus, which is three days' march distant from the Ister for one travelling towards the Haemus.

2. Syrmus, king of the Triballians, having long before learned of Alexander's expedition, sent the women and children of the Triballians ahead to the Ister, bidding them cross the river to one of the islands in it; the island is named Peuce.

3. To this island too the Thracians neighbouring the Triballians had fled long before, as Alexander approached, and Syrmus himself with his people had taken refuge there. But the great mass of the Triballians fled back to the river, to the place from which Alexander had set out the day before.

4. When he learned of their movement, he turned back and led against the Triballians, and came upon them already encamping. Those caught drew up for battle by the wooded glen along the river. Alexander too drew up his phalanx in depth and led it on, ordering the archers and slingers to run out ahead and shoot and sling at the barbarians, in the hope of drawing them out of the glen into the open ground.

5. When they came within range and were struck, they rushed out against the archers, eager to come to close quarters with men who were unprotected. But Alexander, having thus drawn them out of the glen, ordered Philotas to take the cavalry from upper Macedonia and charge against their right wing, where they had advanced furthest in the sally, and stationed Heraclides and Sopolis to lead the cavalry from Bottiaea and Amphipolis against the left wing.

6. The phalanx of the foot, with the rest of the cavalry drawn out in front of the phalanx, he led against the centre. As long as it was a skirmish of missiles on both sides, the Triballians had the worse of it not at all; but when the dense phalanx fell upon them in force, and the cavalry charged no longer with the javelin but thrusting with the very horses, attacking now here, now there, then at last they turned and fled through the glen to the river.

7. Three thousand died in the flight; few were taken alive, both because there was thick woodland before the river and because nightfall robbed the Macedonians of an exact pursuit. Of the Macedonians themselves, Ptolemy says that eleven cavalry and about forty foot were killed.
Chapter 3

1. On the third day after the battle Alexander reached the river Ister, the greatest of the rivers of Europe, traversing the most land and shutting off the most warlike peoples—mostly Celtic, where indeed its sources rise, the last of whom are the Quadi and Marcomanni;

2. then a portion of the Sauromatae, the Iazyges; then the Getae, who believe themselves immortal; then the main body of the Sauromatae; then the Scythians, as far as its mouths, where it empties through five outlets into the Euxine Sea.

3. There he found that warships had come to him from Byzantium through the Euxine and up the river. Filling these with archers and hoplites, he sailed against the island to which the Triballians and Thracians had fled, and tried to force a landing.

4. But the barbarians came down to the river wherever the ships put in; and the ships were few, the force aboard them small, the greater part of the island sheer and hard to attack, and the current of the river beside it, hemmed into a narrow channel, swift and difficult to make way against.

5. So Alexander withdrew the ships and resolved to cross the Ister against the Getae who dwelt beyond it; for he saw many of them gathered on the bank of the Ister, to bar his crossing if he should attempt it—there were some four thousand cavalry and more than ten thousand foot—and at the same time a longing seized him to go beyond the Ister.

6. He himself went aboard the ships; and stuffing with chaff the leather tent-coverings under which they slept, and gathering all the dugout boats he could from the country—of which there was great abundance, since the riverside dwellers use them for fishing in the Ister, and whenever they travel to one another up the river, and many of them for piracy—he collected as many of these as possible and ferried across upon them as many of the army as could be carried in such a fashion. Those who crossed with Alexander were some fifteen hundred cavalry and four thousand foot.
Chapter 4

1. They crossed by night where there was a deep field of standing grain, and so the more easily reached the bank unobserved. At dawn Alexander led on through the grain, ordering the infantry to bend down the corn with their sarissas held aslant, and so advance to the uncultivated ground. The cavalry followed as long as the phalanx went on through the grain;
2. but when they had marched out of the tilled ground, Alexander himself led the cavalry to the right wing, and ordered Nicanor to lead the phalanx in a square.

3. The Getae did not withstand even the first charge of the cavalry; for Alexander's daring seemed to them past belief, that so easily, in a single night, he had crossed the Ister, the greatest of rivers, without bridging the passage; the close array of the phalanx too was fearful, and the charge of the cavalry violent.

4. At first they fled to their city, which lay about a parasang from the Ister; but when they saw Alexander pressing on in haste—the phalanx along the river, lest the foot be encircled anywhere by an ambush of the Getae, and the cavalry in front—the Getae abandoned even their poorly fortified city, taking up on their horses as many of the children and women as the horses could carry,

5. and made off as far as possible from the river into the wilderness. Alexander took the city and all the plunder the Getae had left behind. He gave the plunder to Meleager and Philip to carry back, and himself razed the city; then on the bank of the Ister he sacrificed to Zeus the Saviour, to Heracles, and to the Ister itself, because it had not proved impassable to him, and led all his men back safe to the camp that same day.

6. There envoys came to Alexander, both from the other independent peoples dwelling along the Ister and from Syrmus, king of the Triballians; and there came too men from the Celts settled on the Ionian Gulf—great of body the Celts, and high in their own esteem; and all declared that they had come desiring Alexander's friendship.

7. To all of them Alexander gave pledges and received them. He asked the Celts what among human things they most feared, expecting that his own name had reached even to the Celts and yet further, and that they would say they feared him most of all.

8. But the Celts' answer fell out contrary to his expectation; for, dwelling far from Alexander and inhabiting regions hard to reach, and seeing that Alexander's purpose was bent elsewhere, they said they feared that the sky might one day fall upon them, and that they had come as envoys to Alexander out of admiration, neither from fear nor for advantage. These men he named friends and made allies, and sent them back, remarking only that the Celts were braggarts.
Chapter 5

1. He himself advanced into the country of the Agrianians and Paeonians. There messengers reached him reporting that Cleitus, son of Bardylis, had revolted, and that Glaucias, king of the Taulantians, had joined him; some reported also that the Autariatae would attack him on the march. For these reasons he resolved to break camp in haste.

2. Langarus, king of the Agrianians, who even in Philip's lifetime had plainly favoured Alexander and had sent an embassy to him privately, was now present with the hypaspists, the finest and best-armed men he kept about him.

3. And when he learned that Alexander was inquiring about the Autariatae, who and how many they were, he said there was no need to take account of the Autariatae, for they were the least warlike of the peoples thereabouts; and he himself would invade their country, so that they might be busied about their own affairs. At Alexander's bidding he invaded them, and laid waste their land. So the Autariatae were occupied with their own concerns.

4. Langarus was greatly honoured by Alexander in other ways, and received the gifts esteemed greatest at the court of the king of the Macedonians; and Alexander agreed to give him his sister Cyna in marriage, when he should come to Pella.

5. But Langarus, on returning home, died of a sickness. Alexander, marching along the river Erigon, set out for the city of Pellium; for Cleitus had occupied it as the strongest place in the country. When Alexander came before it, he encamped by the river Eordaicus, intending on the next day to assault the wall.

6. But the men of Cleitus held the heights around the city, which were commanding and wooded, so as to fall upon the Macedonians from every side if they should assault the city; and Glaucias, king of the Taulantians, was not yet present with him.

7. Alexander then advanced upon the city; and the enemy, having sacrificed three boys, an equal number of girls, and three black rams, set out as though to receive the Macedonians at close quarters, but when they came together they abandoned the positions they held, strong though they were, so that their very sacrificial victims were found still lying there.

8. That day, then, having shut them up in the city and encamped by the wall, he resolved to blockade them with a wall of circumvallation. But on the next day Glaucias, king of the Taulantians, arrived with a large force. Then Alexander gave up hope of taking the city with the force at hand, since many warlike men had fled into it and many more would press upon him with Glaucias if he attacked the wall.

9. He sent Philotas, with such of the cavalry as he had, to escort the baggage animals from the camp for foraging. Glaucias, learning of Philotas' movement, marched out against them and occupied the hills around the plain, from which Philotas' men were to forage.

10. When word came to Alexander that the cavalry and baggage animals were in danger if night should overtake them, he himself, taking the hypaspists, the archers, the Agrianians, and about four hundred cavalry, hastened to their aid; the rest of the army he left by the city, lest, if the whole army withdrew, those in the city should sally out and join Glaucias' men.

11. Then Glaucias, perceiving Alexander's approach, abandoned the hills, and Philotas' men got safely back to camp. Yet Cleitus and Glaucias still thought they had caught Alexander in difficult ground;

12. for they held the commanding heights with many cavalry, many javelin-men and slingers, and no small number of hoplites, and those shut up in the city meant to press upon him as he withdrew; while the ground through which Alexander's passage lay seemed narrow and wooded, hemmed on the one side by the river, on the other by a very high mountain with cliffs beneath it, so that not even on a front of four shields could the army pass. Then Alexander drew up his army.
Chapter 6
1. The depth of the phalanx was one hundred and twenty; on either wing he posted two hundred cavalry, and ordered them to keep silence and to take the word of command sharply when it was given.

2. First he signalled the hoplites to raise their spears upright, then at a signal to bring them down to the level for the charge, and now to incline the locked spears to the right, now again to the left. He moved the phalanx itself swiftly forward and led it now to one wing, now to the other.

3. Having thus drawn up and rearranged many formations in a short time, he made on the left a kind of wedge of the phalanx and led it against the enemy. They had long been marvelling at the speed and the good order of his manoeuvres; and now, as Alexander's men came on, they did not stand to receive them, but abandoned the first hills.

4. Alexander ordered the Macedonians to raise the war-cry and to clash their spears upon their shields; and the Taulantians, still more dismayed at the shout, hurriedly led their army back towards the city.

5. Alexander, seeing a few of the enemy holding a hill by which his passage lay, ordered his bodyguards and the Companions about him to take up their shields, mount their horses, and ride at the hill; and on reaching it, if those who held the place stood their ground, half were to leap down from their horses and, mingling with the cavalry, fight on foot.

6. The enemy, seeing Alexander's advance, abandoned the hill and drew off to either side of the mountains. Then Alexander, having seized the hill with the Companions, summoned the Agrianians and the archers, some two thousand in number; and he ordered the hypaspists to cross the river, and after them the battalions of the Macedonians; and as soon as they had crossed, to deploy to the left, so that the phalanx might at once appear dense as it crossed. He himself, on guard, watched from the hill the enemy's movements.

7. They, seeing the force crossing, came down along the mountains to fall upon Alexander's rearmost men as they withdrew. But as they drew near, Alexander himself charged out with his men, and the phalanx raised the war-cry as if advancing through the river; and the enemy, with all bearing down upon them, gave way and fled. In that moment Alexander led the Agrianians and archers at a run towards the river, and was himself the first to cross.

8. When he saw the enemy pressing upon his rearmost men, he set the engines on the bank and ordered them to shoot as far as their missiles would carry, and the archers to shoot from the middle of the river, wading in as well. The men of Glaucias did not dare come within range, and the Macedonians meanwhile crossed the river in safety, so that not a man was lost in their withdrawal.

9. On the third day after this, Alexander, learning that Cleitus and Glaucias were ill encamped, keeping no proper watches in their lines and protected by neither palisade nor ditch, since they supposed he had withdrawn in fear, and that their line was extended to a useless length, crossed the river by night while still unobserved, taking with him the hypaspists, the Agrianians, the archers, and the battalions of Perdiccas and Coenus.

10. The rest of the army had been ordered to follow; but when he saw his chance to attack, he did not wait for all to come up, but launched the archers and Agrianians. Falling upon the enemy unexpectedly and in column upon their flank—where they were weakest and the charge would strike hardest—they killed some still in their beds and easily caught others as they fled, so that many were cut off there and slain, and many in the disorderly and panic-stricken retreat; and not a few were taken alive.

11. Alexander's men pursued as far as the mountains of the Taulantians; and those of the enemy who escaped saved themselves stripped of their arms. Cleitus, having at first fled into the city, set it on fire and made off to Glaucias among the Taulantians.
Chapter 7

1. Meanwhile some of the exiles who had fled from Thebes, entering the city by night at the invitation of certain men within who wished to revolt, seized and killed Amyntas and Timolaus, two of those holding the Cadmeia, who suspected nothing hostile, outside the citadel.

2. Coming before the assembly, they urged the Thebans to revolt from Alexander, holding out before them the fair old names of liberty, and the prospect of being rid at last of the heavy hand of the Macedonians. They carried the more conviction with the people by insisting that Alexander had died among the Illyrians;

3. for this report was widespread and came from many quarters—both because he had been absent no short time and because no message had come from him—so that, as is wont to happen in such cases, men, not knowing the truth, guessed at what was most to their liking.

4. When Alexander learned of the Thebans' doings, it seemed to him by no means a matter to neglect, since he had long held the city of the Athenians in suspicion, and reckoned the Thebans' venture no slight one, if the Lacedaemonians, long since disaffected in spirit, and certain others in the Peloponnese, and the Aetolians, who were unsteady, should join the Thebans in revolt.

5. Leading on past Eordaea and Elimiotis and the heights of Stymphaea and Paravaea, on the seventh day he reached Pelinna in Thessaly. Setting out thence, on the sixth day he burst into Boeotia, so that the Thebans did not learn he had passed within Thermopylae until he was at Onchestus with his whole army.

6. Even then those who had brought about the revolt asserted that an army had come from Macedonia under Antipater, and insisted that Alexander himself was dead, and were angry with those who reported that this very Alexander was approaching; it was, they said, another Alexander, the son of Aëropus, who had come.

7. Alexander, setting out from Onchestus, on the next day advanced upon the city of the Thebans by the precinct of Iolaus, where he encamped, still allowing the Thebans time, in case they should repent of their ill counsels and send an embassy to him.

8. But so far were they from offering any opening towards an agreement that their cavalry and no small number of light troops ran out from the city as far as the camp and skirmished against the outposts, and killed a few of the Macedonians.

9. Alexander sent out some of the light troops and archers to check their sally, and these easily checked them when they were already coming up to the very camp. On the next day, taking his whole army and going round towards the gates leading to Eleutherae and Attica, even then he did not come up to the walls themselves, but encamped not far from the Cadmeia, so that aid from the Macedonians might be near for those holding the Cadmeia.

10. For the Thebans had been blockading the Cadmeia with a double stockade, so that none from without could help those shut up within, nor could the garrison sally out and do them any harm whenever they engaged the enemy outside. Alexander—for he still wished to come to terms with the Thebans through friendship rather than through danger—lingered, encamped by the Cadmeia.

11. Then those of the Thebans who thought best for the common good were eager to go out to Alexander and obtain pardon for the Theban people for their revolt; but the exiles and those who had recalled them, deeming they would meet with no clemency from Alexander—some of them being moreover Boeotarchs—urged the people altogether to war. Yet not even so did Alexander assault the city.
Chapter 8

1. But Ptolemy son of Lagus says that Perdiccas, posted in advance to guard the camp with his own battalion, not far from the enemy's stockade, without waiting for Alexander's signal for battle, was himself the first to attack the stockade, and tearing it apart broke in upon the Theban outpost.

2. Following him, Amyntas son of Andromenes, because he was drawn up with Perdiccas, led on his own battalion too, when he saw Perdiccas had advanced within the stockade. Seeing this, Alexander, lest they be cut off alone and endangered by the Thebans, led on the rest of the army.

3. He signalled the archers and Agrianians to run within the stockade, but kept the royal guard and the hypaspists still outside. There Perdiccas, forcing his way to pass within the second stockade, was himself struck down and fell, and was carried off in a bad state to the camp, and barely recovered from his wound. His men, however, breaking in along with Alexander's archers, drove the Thebans into the hollow road leading by the Heracleium.

4. They followed the Thebans as far as they retreated towards the Heracleium; but when the Thebans turned again with a shout, a flight of the Macedonians ensued. Eurybotas the Cretan, the captain of the archers, fell, and about seventy of the archers themselves; the rest fled to the Macedonian royal guard and the royal hypaspists.

5. At this moment Alexander, seeing his own men in flight and the Thebans in their pursuit broken in array, charged them with the phalanx in close order. They drove the Thebans within the gates; and the Thebans' flight became so headlong that, thrust through the gates into the city, they could not close them in time. For along with them burst within the wall those of the Macedonians who pressed close upon the fugitives, the walls being for the most part stripped of defenders because of the many outposts.

6. Passing into the Cadmeia, some came out thence by the Ampheion together with those holding the Cadmeia into the rest of the city, while others, climbing the walls—now held by those who had burst in with the fugitives—ran down into the marketplace at full speed.

7. For a little while those of the Thebans posted at the Ampheion held their ground; but when the Macedonians, and Alexander appearing now here, now there, pressed upon them from every side, the Theban cavalry broke through the city into the plain and escaped, while the foot saved themselves each as he could.

8. Then in their fury—not so much the Macedonians as the Phocians and Plataeans and the other Boeotians—they slew the Thebans, who no longer defended themselves, in utter disorder: falling upon some in their houses, others who had turned to resist, others as they supplicated at the shrines, sparing neither women nor children.
Chapter 9

1. This calamity of a Greek city, by the greatness of the captured city and the swiftness of the event, struck both the sufferers and the doers, and no less the other Greeks than those who shared in the deed itself, with consternation.

2. For the disaster that befell the Athenians at Sicily, even though in the number of the dead it brought no smaller a calamity upon the city, yet because their army was destroyed far from home, and was mostly allied rather than their own, and because their city was left to them, so that afterwards they long held out in the war against the Lacedaemonians and their allies and the Great King—that disaster neither gave the sufferers themselves an equal sense of the calamity nor caused the other Greeks the like consternation at the blow.

3. And again the Athenian defeat at Aegospotami was a naval one, and the city, reduced to humility by nothing else than the demolition of the long walls, the surrender of most of her ships, and the loss of her empire, nevertheless preserved her ancestral form of government, and not long after recovered her former power, so as to rebuild the long walls and again command the sea, and in their turn save from the utmost dangers the very Lacedaemonians, then so fearful to them and so nearly the destroyers of their city.

4. The Lacedaemonians' disaster at Leuctra and Mantinea struck them by the unexpectedness of the calamity rather than by the number of the dead; and the assault upon Sparta made by the Boeotians and Arcadians under Epaminondas terrified the Lacedaemonians themselves and their associates more by the strangeness of the sight than by the exactness of the danger.

5. The capture of Plataea, again, by the smallness of the city and the fewness of those caught in it—since most had long before escaped to Athens—was no great calamity. And the capture of Melos and Scione brought something of an island nature, but afforded no great shock to the whole of Greece.

6. But for the Thebans the suddenness of their revolt, made with no calculation, and the capture coming swiftly and without toil to those who took the city, and the great slaughter—such as comes from kinsmen pursuing an ancient enmity—and the utter enslavement of a city pre-eminent at that time among the Greeks in power and in military repute, were not unreasonably referred to the wrath of heaven;

7. as though the Thebans were at long last paying this penalty for their betrayal of the Greeks in the Persian War, for their seizure of Plataea during a truce and the utter enslavement of its city, for the slaughter, un-Greek and brought about through the Thebans, of those who had surrendered themselves to the Lacedaemonians, and for the desolation of the very ground on which the Greeks, drawn up against the Medes, had thrust the danger from Hellas; and because the Thebans had themselves by their vote sought to destroy the Athenians, when the question of enslaving their city was proposed among the allies of the Lacedaemonians.

8. For even before the calamity many portents were said to have been sent from heaven, which at the time were disregarded, but which afterwards memory referred to a reckoning, as having long foreshown what was to come.

9. To the allies who had shared in the work, to whom Alexander entrusted the settlement of Theban affairs, it was resolved to hold the Cadmeia with a garrison, to raze the city to the ground, to apportion the land—save what was sacred—among the allies, and to enslave the children and women and whoever of the Thebans was left, except the priests and priestesses and those who were guest-friends of Philip or Alexander or proxenoi of the Macedonians.

10. They say too that Alexander preserved the house of the poet Pindar and Pindar's descendants, out of reverence for Pindar. Besides this, the allies resolved to restore and fortify Orchomenus and Plataea.
Chapter 10

1. When the Thebans' fate was reported to the other Greeks, the Arcadians, as many as had set out from home to help the Thebans, condemned to death those who had induced them to the aid; the Eleans recalled their exiles, because they were well-disposed to Alexander;

2. the Aetolians, sending embassies by tribes, begged to obtain pardon, because they too had made some stir in response to the Thebans' messages; and the Athenians, while the Great Mysteries were being held, when some of the Thebans arrived straight from the deed, were so dismayed that they abandoned the Mysteries and brought their goods in from the fields into the city.

3. The people, gathering in assembly, on the motion of Demades chose ten envoys from all the Athenians and sent them to Alexander—such men as they knew were most acceptable to him—to announce, though out of season, that the Athenian people rejoiced he had returned safe from the Illyrians and Triballians, and that he had punished the Thebans for their revolt.

4. He answered the embassy graciously in other respects, but wrote a letter to the people demanding the surrender of Demosthenes and Lycurgus and their party; he demanded too Hypereides, Polyeuctus, Chares, Charidemus, Ephialtes, Diotimus, and Moerocles;

5. for he declared these men responsible both for the disaster the city suffered at Chaeronea and for the offences committed afterwards, on Philip's death, against himself and against Philip; and he showed that they were no less responsible for the Thebans' revolt than the Thebans themselves who had risen.

6. The Athenians, however, did not give up the men, but sent another embassy to Alexander, begging him to remit his anger against those demanded. And Alexander relented, whether out of reverence for the city, or out of his eagerness for the expedition into Asia, not wishing to leave anything suspect among the Greeks. Charidemus alone, of those demanded and not surrendered, he ordered into exile; and Charidemus fled to Asia, to the Great King Darius.
Chapter 11

1. Having accomplished these things, Alexander returned to Macedonia. He offered to Olympian Zeus the sacrifice established since the time of Archelaus, and held the Olympic games at Aegae; some say he held games in honour of the Muses as well.

2. At this time it was reported that the statue of Orpheus, son of Oeagrus the Thracian, in Pieria sweated continuously; and the seers gave various interpretations of the portent, but Aristander, a man of Telmissus and a seer, bade Alexander take heart; for it signified that poets of epic and song, and all who busy themselves with music, would have much labour in composing and singing of Alexander and Alexander's deeds.

3. At the beginning of spring he marched towards the Hellespont, entrusting affairs in Macedonia and among the Greeks to Antipater, while he himself led foot, with light troops and archers, not much more than thirty thousand, and over five thousand cavalry. His march lay by the Cercinitis lake towards Amphipolis and the mouths of the river Strymon.
4. Crossing the Strymon, he passed Mount Pangaeum, by the road towards Abdera and Maroneia, Greek cities founded upon the sea. Thence he came to the river Hebrus and crossed it easily.

Not many days later, as Alexander again brought up his engines against the inner brick wall and was himself overseeing the work, there was a sally in full force from the city: some by the ruined wall, where Alexander himself was posted, others by the Triple Gate, where the Macedonians were not at all expecting it.

2. The one party flung torches at the engines and whatever else might kindle a flame and raise it high; but as Alexander's men charged stoutly upon them, and the engines from the towers hurled great stones and shot out missiles, they were without difficulty turned and fled into the city.

3. There was no little slaughter here, in proportion as more had run out and with greater daring. For some, coming to close quarters with the Macedonians, were killed; others perished about the fallen wall, the passage being too narrow for their numbers and the ruins of the wall affording them difficult crossing.

4. Against those who had run out by the Triple Gate Ptolemy, the royal bodyguard, came out, leading with him the battalion of Adaeus and Timander and some of the light troops; and these too without difficulty routed the men from the city.

5. It befell these also, in their withdrawal, fleeing across the narrow bridge made over the ditch, that the bridge itself was crushed by the press, and many of them, falling into the ditch, perished, some trampled by their own men, others struck from above by the Macedonians.

6. The greatest slaughter befell at the very gates, because the closing of the gates, fearful and made before the right moment—for they dreaded lest the Macedonians, pressing close upon the fugitives, should burst in with them—shut out many even of their own from entrance, whom the Macedonians slew at the very walls.

7. The city came near to being taken, had not Alexander recalled the army, still wishing to save Halicarnassus, in case something friendly should be offered by the Halicarnassians. Of the men from the city about a thousand died, and of Alexander's about forty, among them Ptolemy the bodyguard, Clearchus the captain of archers, Adaeus the chiliarch, and others of the not undistinguished Macedonians.
Chapter 23

1. Then the Persian commanders, Orontobates and Memnon, meeting together and judging from the circumstances that they could not hold out long under the siege—seeing part of the wall already fallen, part shaken down, and many of the soldiers either killed in the sallies or disabled by wounds—

2. with these things in mind, about the second watch of the night they set fire to the wooden tower which they had built to face the enemy's engines, and to the porticoes in which their missiles were stored. They threw fire also upon the houses near the wall;

3. and the flame caught some of these too, carried far from the porticoes and the tower, the wind also driving it that way. Of the men, some withdrew to the citadel on the island, others to Salmacis, the citadel so called.

4. When this was reported to Alexander by some who deserted from the work, and he himself saw the great fire, though it was about midnight that this was happening, even so he led out the Macedonians and killed those still setting fire to the city, but ordered that whoever of the Halicarnassians was found in the houses should be spared. Day was now breaking, and he saw the citadels

5. which the Persians and mercenaries had occupied; these he gave up trying to besiege, reckoning that the siege would cost him no little delay by the nature of the ground, and that it was of no great moment now that he had already taken the whole city.

6. Having buried those who had died in the night, he ordered those in charge of the engines to take them away to Tralles; and he himself razed the city to the ground, and leaving a garrison of this and the rest of Caria—three thousand mercenary foot and about two hundred cavalry, with Ptolemy as their commander—set out for Phrygia.

7. As satrap of all Caria he appointed Ada, daughter of Hecatomnus and wife of Hidrieus, who, being also her brother, had lived with her according to the custom of the Carians. Hidrieus, dying, entrusted affairs to her, it being established in Asia ever since Semiramis that women too should rule over men. But Pixodarus drove her from power and held affairs himself.

8. When Pixodarus died, Orontobates, sent by the King, held the rule of the Carians, being Pixodarus' son-in-law. Ada held Alinda alone, one of the strongest places in Caria; and when Alexander invaded Caria she came to meet him, surrendering Alinda and adopting Alexander as her son. Alexander entrusted Alinda to her and did not disdain the name of son; and when he had taken Halicarnassus and mastered the rest of Caria, he gave her the rule of the whole.
Chapter 24

1. There were some of the Macedonians serving with Alexander who had married shortly before the expedition; and Alexander judged that these too were not to be neglected, but sent them away from Caria to winter in Macedonia with their wives, appointing over them Ptolemy son of Seleucus, one of the royal bodyguards, and of the generals Coenus son of Polemocrates and Meleager son of Neoptolemus, because they too were among the newly wed;

2. with orders that, when they themselves returned and brought back those sent with them, they should levy as many cavalry and foot from the country as possible. And by this act, if by any other, Alexander won favour among the Macedonians. He sent also Cleander son of Polemocrates to the Peloponnese to gather soldiers.

3. Parmenion he sent to Sardis, giving him a regiment of the Companions, the Thessalian cavalry, the other allies, and the wagons to lead; and he bade him advance from Sardis into Phrygia. He himself went towards Lycia and Pamphylia, so as, by mastering the coast, to render the enemy's fleet useless.

4. First on the way he took at the first assault Hyparna, a strong place holding a garrison of foreign mercenaries; and the mercenaries from the citadel went out under truce. Then, invading Lycia, he won over the Telmissians by agreement, and crossing the river Xanthus took Pinara, the city of Xanthus, and Patara, which were surrendered, and about thirty other smaller towns.

5. Having done this, at the very height of winter he invaded the country called Milyas, which is part of greater Phrygia but at that time was reckoned with Lycia, so ordered by the Great King. There envoys of the Phaselites came concerning friendship and to crown Alexander with a golden crown; and most of the lower Lycians sent embassies treating for the same.

6. Alexander ordered the Phaselites and Lycians to surrender their cities to those sent for this purpose; and they were all surrendered. He himself, coming a little later to Phaselis, helped them take a strong fort built against their country by the Pisidians, from which the barbarians, setting out, did much harm to those of the Phaselites who tilled the land.
Chapter 25

1. While he was still about Phaselis, it was reported that Alexander son of Aëropus was plotting against him—a man who was among the Companions and at that time commanded the Thessalian cavalry. This Alexander was brother of Heromenes and Arrhabaeus, who had shared in the murder of Philip;

2. and at that earlier time, when he was under accusation, Alexander acquitted him, because he had come among the first of his friends to him when Philip died, and putting on his breastplate had accompanied him into the palace; and afterwards he kept him about himself in honour, sending him as general to Thrace, and when Calas the commander of the Thessalian cavalry was sent off to a satrapy, appointed him to command the Thessalian cavalry. The matter of the plot was reported thus.

3. Darius, when Amyntas, deserting to him, brought certain messages and letters from this Alexander, sent down to the coast Sisines, a Persian among his trusted men, ostensibly to Atizyes the satrap of Phrygia, but in truth to confer with this Alexander and to give him pledges that, if he should kill King Alexander, Darius would make him king of Macedonia and would give him, besides the kingdom, a thousand talents of gold.

4. But Sisines, captured by Parmenion, told Parmenion the purpose for which he had been sent; and Parmenion sent him under guard to Alexander, and Alexander learned the same from him. Gathering his friends, he laid before them the question what should be decided about Alexander.

5. And it seemed to the Companions that he had not formerly been well advised in entrusting the strongest of his cavalry to an untrustworthy man, and that now he should put him out of the way quickly, before he should become more acceptable to the Thessalians and make some revolt with them. Something divine too alarmed them.

6. For while Alexander was still besieging Halicarnassus, as he was resting at midday, a swallow flew about over his head, twittering loudly and settling now here, now there on the bed, singing more noisily than was its wont;

7. and he, being weary, could not be roused from sleep, but, troubled by the sound, brushed the swallow gently away with his hand; yet it was so far from flying off when struck that it settled on Alexander's very head and did not leave off until Alexander was fully awake.

8. Alexander, not making light of the swallow, communicated it to Aristander of Telmissus, the seer; and Aristander said it signified a plot from one of his friends, and signified too that it would be brought to light; for the swallow is a bird that lives among men and is friendly to them and more talkative than any other bird.

9. Putting these things together with what came from the Persian, he sent to Parmenion Amphoterus, Alexander's son and Craterus' brother. He sent with him some of the Pergaeans to guide the way; and Amphoterus, putting on local dress so as not to be recognized on the road, reached Parmenion unobserved;

10. and he brought no letters from Alexander—for it seemed best not to write in plain words about such a matter—but reported by word of mouth what had been enjoined upon him. And so this Alexander was arrested and kept under guard.
Chapter 26

1. Alexander, setting out from Phaselis, sent part of his army through the mountains to Perge, where the Thracians had made a road for him through a passage otherwise difficult and long; he himself led those about him along the sea, by the shore. This road is passable only when the winds blow from the north; if south winds prevail, it is impossible to travel along the shore.

2. But after south winds, strong north winds, not without the divine help—as he himself and those about him interpreted it—blew up and made the passage easy and swift. As he advanced from Perge, envoys of the Aspendians, with full powers, met him on the road, surrendering the city, but asking that he not bring in a garrison.

3. As to the garrison they obtained their request and departed; but he ordered them to give the army fifty talents for pay, and the horses which they reared as tribute for the King. Agreeing to hand over both the silver and the horses, they departed. Alexander went on towards Side.

4. The Sidetans are Cymaeans, from Cyme in Aeolis; and they tell this story of themselves: that when the first colonists sent from Cyme put in to that land and disembarked to found a city, they at once forgot the Greek tongue, and immediately uttered a barbarous speech—not that of the neighbouring barbarians, but a peculiar one of their own, never before existing; and ever since the Sidetans have spoken a barbarous tongue unlike that of their neighbours.

5. Leaving a garrison in Side, he advanced upon Syllium, a strong place holding a garrison of foreign mercenaries and of the native barbarians themselves. But he was unable to take Syllium by an offhand assault; and when it was reported to him on the road that the Aspendians were unwilling to perform any of the agreed terms—neither to hand over the horses to those sent, nor to count out the money—and that they had brought their goods from the country into the city, shut the gates against Alexander's men, and were repairing the walls where they had decayed, on learning this he set out against Aspendus.
Chapter 27

1. The greater part of Aspendus is built upon a strong and sheer height, and beside the very height the river Eurymedon flows; but they had also, around the height in the low ground, no few dwellings, with a wall, not great, thrown round them.

2. The wall, at once, when they learned Alexander was approaching, was abandoned by all who dwelt there, along with the houses which, built in the low ground, they did not think they could defend; and they themselves fled together to the height. When Alexander arrived with his force, passing within the deserted wall, he encamped in the houses left empty by the Aspendians.

3. The Aspendians, seeing Alexander himself come beyond their expectation, and the camp all around them on every side, sent envoys begging to come to terms on the same conditions as before. Alexander, seeing the place strong, and himself not prepared for a long siege, even so did not agree with them on the same terms;

4. but ordered them to give as hostages their most powerful men, and the horses they had before agreed upon, and a hundred talents instead of the fifty, and to obey the satrap appointed by Alexander, and to pay tribute yearly to the Macedonians, and to submit to arbitration concerning the land which, belonging to their neighbours, they were accused of holding by force. When they had conceded all this to him, he set out for Perge, and thence made for Phrygia;
5. his march lay past the city of Telmissus. These people are by race Pisidian barbarians, and dwell in a very lofty place, sheer on every side, and the road past the city is difficult.

6. For a mountain reaches down from the city as far as the road, and there breaks off in the road itself, while facing it is another mountain no less sheer; and these mountains make as it were gates upon the road, so that even a small garrison holding these mountains can make the passage impossible. And then the Telmissians, having come out in full force, held both mountains.

7. Seeing this, Alexander ordered the Macedonians to encamp there, just as they were, judging that the Telmissians would not remain in full force when they saw his men bivouacking, but that most of them would withdraw to the city, which was near, leaving only a guard upon the mountains. And it fell out as he had guessed; for most of them went off, but the guards remained.

8. Against these he at once led the archers, the battalions of the javelin-men, and such of the hoplites as were lighter-armed. They did not stand to be shot at, but abandoned the place; and Alexander, crossing the narrows, encamped near the city.
Chapter 28

1. There came to him envoys of the Selgians. These too are Pisidian barbarians and dwell in a great city, and are themselves warlike; but because they happened to be enemies of the Telmissians from of old, they had sent an embassy to Alexander concerning friendship. With these Alexander made a treaty, and thereafter found them faithful in all things.

2. Despairing of taking Telmissus in a short time, he set out for Sagalassus. This too was no small city; Pisidians inhabited it as well, and, all the Pisidians being warlike, these were thought to be the most warlike of all; and at that time they had occupied the hill before the city, which was no less strong than the wall for fighting from, and awaited the attack.

3. Alexander drew up the Macedonian phalanx thus: on the right wing, where he himself was posted, he had the hypaspists, and next to these the foot-companions, extending the line as far as the left, with the command of his own portion of the array assigned to each general for that day.

4. On the left he posted as commander Amyntas son of Arrhabaeus. There were posted in advance, on the right wing, the archers and the Agrianians; on the left, the Thracian javelin-men, led by Sitalces; for his cavalry was of no use in the difficult ground. The Telmissians, who had come to their aid, were drawn up with the Pisidians.

5. When Alexander's men, having attacked the mountain held by the Pisidians, were at the very steepest part of the ascent, the barbarians fell upon them in companies on either flank, where the approach was easiest for themselves and most difficult for the enemy. The archers, being neither well-armed nor having drawn near first, they routed; but the Agrianians held.

6. For the Macedonian phalanx was now drawing near, and before it Alexander was seen. When the battle came to close quarters, the barbarians, being unarmoured, were borne against hoplites, and, wounded on every side, fell; then they gave way.

7. About five hundred of them were killed; for being nimble and skilled in the ground, they withdrew without difficulty, while the Macedonians, by the weight of their arms and ignorance of the roads, were not bold in pursuit.

8. Alexander, keeping close to the fugitives, took their city by storm. Of his own men, Cleander the general of the archers died, and about twenty others. Alexander then led against the rest of the Pisidians; some of their forts he took by force, others he won over by agreement.
Chapter 29

1. Thence he went towards Phrygia, past the lake named Ascania, in which salt forms of itself, and the inhabitants use it and have no need of the sea for this purpose; and on the fifth day he reached Celaenae. At Celaenae there was a citadel, sheer on every side, held by a garrison from the satrap of Phrygia—a thousand Carians and a hundred Greek mercenaries.

2. These sent an embassy to Alexander, undertaking that, if help did not reach them by a day on which they agreed—naming the day—they would surrender the place. And this seemed to Alexander more profitable than to besiege a citadel altogether impossible to assail.

3. He left a garrison of about fifteen hundred soldiers at Celaenae. Remaining there ten days, and appointing Antigonus son of Philip satrap of Phrygia, and Balacrus son of Amyntas as general over the allies in his place, he himself set out for Gordium. He sent word to Parmenion to come there to meet him with his force; and Parmenion came with the force.

4. The newly wed who had been sent to Macedonia came to Gordium, and with them another army, levied afresh, which Ptolemy son of Seleucus, Coenus son of Polemocrates, and Meleager son of Neoptolemus led: three thousand Macedonian foot, about three hundred cavalry, two hundred Thessalian cavalry, and a hundred and fifty Eleans, led by Alcias the Elean.

5. Gordium is in Hellespontine Phrygia, and lies upon the river Sangarius; the sources of the Sangarius are in Phrygia, but it flows through the country of the Bithynian Thracians and empties into the Euxine Sea. There too an embassy of the Athenians came to Alexander, begging him to release to them the prisoners who had been taken at the river Granicus, Athenians serving with the Persians, and were then bound in Macedonia with the two thousand;

6. and concerning these they departed at that time unsuccessful. For it did not seem safe to Alexander, while the war against the Persian still continued, to relax anything of the fear among the Greeks who had not disdained to campaign against Greece on behalf of the barbarians; but he answered that when present affairs had gone well, then they might come as envoys concerning the same matter.
